query: Using the reported HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high-entropy alloy as the starting material and its quasi-static properties—786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain—as the baseline, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to overcome limited strain hardening, poor uniform deformability, and rapid failure as strain rate increases under adiabatic dynamic deformation? Specify the intervention and mechanism, predict changes relative to the baseline in strength, uniform deformation, localization resistance, and impact-induced energy release, define the strain-rate and loading conditions over which the prediction applies, cite supporting evidence from the reported refractory-alloy literature, and describe a matched baseline-versus-intervention experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial alloying of HfZrTiTa0.53 with a moderate addition (~5-10 at. %) of tungsten (W) will induce a dual‐phase microstructure featuring uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitates that enhance dynamic strain hardening, improve uniform plastic deformation, delay adiabatic shear localization, and increase impact-induced energy absorption compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy with composition HfZrTiTa0.53 that, under quasi‐static conditions, exhibits a yield strength of 786 MPa, compressive strength of 1314 MPa, and 13.5% fracture strain, but shows limited strain hardening and rapid failure at high strain rates.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled amount (approximately 5-10 at. %) of tungsten into the HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy via arc-melting followed by homogenization and appropriate heat treatment to promote the formation of nanoscale W-rich precipitates within a modified, dual-phase (matrix plus coherent precipitate) microstructure.
generation.conditions: Dynamic adiabatic deformation under compressive loading at strain rates between approximately 1300 s⁻¹ and 2100 s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: A dual-phase microstructure where nanoscale tungsten-rich precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion and enhance dislocation storage, thereby increasing work hardening and retarding the onset of shear localization.
generation.mechanism: W addition increases the overall melting point and provides solid-solution strengthening; it also promotes the precipitation of coherent intermetallic phases (e.g., B2 or similar) that act as additional obstacles to dislocation glide. This enhances dynamic strain hardening, facilitates a more uniform distribution of strain, delays adiabatic shear band formation, and increases the alloy’s capacity to absorb impact energy during high-rate deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy is expected to show a dynamic increase in yield and compressive strength by roughly 10-20%, a higher uniform deformation (with an effective increase in fracture strain by 20-30% under dynamic loading), and a greater capacity for impact-induced energy release due to improved strain hardening and delayed localization.
generation.baseline: The unmodified HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy, which at quasi-static conditions exhibits 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain but suffers from limited strain hardening and rapid failure under adiabatic high strain rate loading.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvements are expected to be significant under adiabatic dynamic loading conditions (strain rates of ~1300-2100 s⁻¹). Under quasi-static or non-adiabatic conditions, the modifications may have minimal impact on the mechanical behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvements is uncertain and may depend on the optimal tungsten content, the resulting precipitate morphology, and the heat treatment parameters. Further experimental optimization is required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: (1) the baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy and (2) the modified alloy with ~5-10 at.% tungsten addition. Use identical processing (arc-melting, homogenization, and heat treatment) to ensure comparable microstructures aside from the intended intervention. Subject both sets to dynamic compressive testing using a Split-Hopkinson Pressure Bar apparatus at strain rates of 1300 to 2100 s⁻¹ under adiabatic conditions.
measurements: Dynamic yield strength and compressive strength from stress–strain curves
Fracture strain and strain hardening rate during dynamic loading
High-resolution microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, SEM) to confirm the presence and distribution of tungsten-rich precipitates
Observation of adiabatic shear band formation
Impact-induced energy absorption via standardized impact tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-modified alloy does not demonstrate statistically significant improvements (at least a 10% increase in dynamic strength and a 20-30% improvement in uniform deformation and energy absorption) compared to the baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to show a dual-phase structure with effective nanoscale precipitates, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The quasi-static compressive stress–strain curves of the alloys with varying W contents are presented in Figure 2a. For the W0 alloy, the yield strength (σYS) and the ultimate strength (σUS) are approximately 1620 MPa and 1810 MPa, respectively, with an elongation of ~22%. Serrated steps observed in the stress–strain curve of W0 suggest a susceptibility to plastic instability. The introduction of W into the alloy preserves the high yield strength while significantly improving both fracture strength and fracture strain []. For example, the W13 alloy demonstrates a yield strength of 1650 MPa, along with an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa and a fracture strain of 32%. Figure 2b presents the dynamic engineering stress–strain curves of alloys with varying W contents, tested at high strain rates (2000 s−1) and at room temperature. Under dynamic conditions, the yield strength of each alloy is significantly enhanced compared with the quasi-static conditions. Notably, while the W0 and W8 alloys exhibit poor dynamic plasticity with elongations below 10%, the W13 and W18 alloys demonstrate superior dynamic mechanical properties, achieving ultra-high dynamic yield strengths (exceeding 2200 MPa)

This study demonstrates that the addition of W significantly enhances the mechanical properties of TiZrMo alloys, with the phase ratio effectively being controlled by adjusting the elemental composition. As a result, a dual-phase Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA was successfully fabricated and subjected to comprehensive quasi-static and dynamic loading experiments to evaluate its energy release capability and mechanical properties for potential structural applications. The Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA demonstrated exceptional quasi-static mechanical performance, with a yield strength of 1490 MPa, an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa, and a fracture strain of 30%. Under dynamic loading at a strain rate of 3000 s−1, the alloy exhibited an even higher ultimate strength of 2300 MPa and maintained a fracture strain of 24%, showcasing its remarkable ability to retain plasticity under extreme conditions. Additionally, the Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA displayed significant chemical energy release and a high energy release capacity. In this work, the effect of strain rate on the microstructural evolution and compression behavior of the dual-phase AlCrFe2Ni2 alloy was studied. The main conclusions are as follows: The as-cast AlCrFe2Ni2 alloy is composed of a mixture of Fe,Ni-enriched FCC phases, disordered Fe,Cr-enriched BCC phases, and ordered Al,Ni-enriched B2 phases. The AlCrFe2Ni2 alloy shows excellent compressive properties under quasi-static deformation. The yield strength exceeds 600 MPa while the compressive strength is more than 3000 MPa at the compression rates of 30%. The ultimate compression stresses are 1522 MPa, 1816 MPa, and 1925 MPa with compression strains about 12.8%, 14.7%, and 18.2% at strain rates of 1300 s−1, 1700 s−1, and 2100 s−1, respectively. Strain rate sensitivity ranges from 0.0089 at low strain (10−4 s−1–100 s−1) to 0.42 at high strain rates (1300 s−1–2100 s−1), which is due to the phonon drag effect at high strains. At high-strain-rate compression, a adiabatic shear phenomenon occurs. The adiabatic shear bands formed by dynamic recrystallization due to the conflicting processes of strain rate hardening and heat softening.
